text:
Typical change-management lifecycle

Diagram
flowchart LR
    A[Capture changed requirement] --> B[Review and approve]
    B --> C[Assess design and dependencies]
    C --> D[Update design and configuration]
    D --> E[Modify versioned code]
    E --> F[Run automated and manual tests]
    F --> G{Tests and reviews pass?}
    G -->|No| C
    G -->|Yes| H[Promote through environments]
    H --> I[Deploy with controlled release]
    I --> J[Monitor and verify]
    J --> K{Healthy?}
    K -->|No| L[Rollback or remediate]
    L --> C
    K -->|Yes| M[Close change and retain audit history]

Most platforms connect requirements to tracked work items, assess architectural and dependency impacts, preserve code and configuration changes in version control, run regression, integration, security, and acceptance tests, and deploy through development, test, staging, and production environments using approvals or CI/CD automation. Safer releases may use feature flags, canary or blue-green deployment, monitoring, and rollback. The platform name or documentation is required to confirm its exact workflow, tools, approval gates, traceability, and deployment strategy.
limitations: The platform is unidentified, so this is a general lifecycle rather than a platform-specific description.
